prompt: According to rule 1 for disubstituted benzenes, what happens when the directing effects of the two groups reinforce each other?

choices.text: Both groups direct to the same position, so a single product forms
The more powerful activator wins, but a mixture of products usually forms
choices.why: That's rule 2, for groups whose directing effects oppose each other.

choices.text: The two groups cancel, so no further substitution occurs
choices.why: Reinforcing groups make the outcome straightforward: substitution occurs at the position both direct to.

choices.text: Substitution occurs between the two groups
choices.why: Rule 3 says substitution rarely occurs between the two groups of a meta-disubstituted ring, because that site is too hindered.

explanation: Rule 1: if the directing effects of the two groups reinforce each other, the situation is straightforward. In p-nitrotoluene, both the methyl and the nitro group direct further substitution to the same position (ortho to the methyl = meta to the nitro), so a single product forms.

prompt: What product forms when p-nitrotoluene is treated with Br2 and FeBr3?

choices.text: 2-Bromo-4-nitrotoluene
3-Bromo-4-nitrotoluene
choices.why: That puts the bromine ortho to the nitro group and meta to the methyl group, a position neither group directs to.

choices.text: A mixture of 2-bromo- and 3-bromo-4-nitrotoluene
choices.why: The two groups reinforce each other, so a single product forms, with bromine ortho to the methyl group.

choices.text: No product, because the nitro group deactivates the ring too much
choices.why: The methyl group activates the position next to it, and the reaction gives 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene.

explanation: In p-nitrotoluene, the methyl group directs ortho (its para position is taken) and the nitro group directs meta. Both point to the same position, ortho to the methyl and meta to the nitro, so bromination gives a single product, 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene (rule 1).

prompt: How many different monobromination products form when p-nitrotoluene is brominated with Br2 and FeBr3?
explanation: The methyl and nitro groups both direct to the positions ortho to the methyl (meta to the nitro). Those two positions are equivalent, so a single product, 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene, forms.

prompt: According to rule 2, what happens when the directing effects of the two groups on a disubstituted benzene oppose each other?

choices.text: The stronger activator dominates, but mixtures often form
The more strongly deactivating group controls the orientation
choices.why: It's the stronger activator, not the stronger deactivator, that dominates.

choices.text: A single product always forms, directed by the group closer to the reacting position
choices.why: Mixtures of products are often formed when the groups oppose each other.

choices.text: No substitution occurs, because the two effects cancel
choices.why: Substitution still occurs; the more powerful activating group mainly decides where.

explanation: Rule 2: if the directing effects of the two groups oppose each other, the more powerful activating group has the dominant influence, but mixtures of products are often formed. Bromination of p-methylphenol, for example, gives primarily 2-bromo-4-methylphenol.

prompt: What is the main product of the bromination of p-methylphenol (Br2, FeBr3)?

choices.text: 2-Bromo-4-methylphenol
3-Bromo-4-methylphenol
choices.why: That puts bromine ortho to the methyl group. –OH is the more powerful activator, so bromine goes ortho to –OH.

choices.text: 4-Bromophenol, by replacement of the methyl group
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen, so the methyl group stays.

choices.text: Equal amounts of 2-bromo- and 3-bromo-4-methylphenol
choices.why: The groups oppose each other, and the more powerful activator, –OH, dominates.

explanation: In p-methylphenol, –OH directs to the positions ortho to itself, and –CH3 directs to the positions ortho to itself. The effects oppose each other, and –OH is a more powerful activator than –CH3, so bromination yields primarily 2-bromo-4-methylphenol (rule 2).

prompt: According to rule 3, why does further substitution rarely occur between the two groups of a meta-disubstituted benzene?

choices.text: The site between the two groups is too hindered
Neither group directs to that position
choices.why: In many meta-disubstituted rings, such as m-chlorotoluene, both groups do direct there. The site is simply too hindered.

choices.text: That position is deactivated by resonance withdrawal from both groups
choices.why: The section's reason is steric: the site between the groups is too hindered.

choices.text: The hydrogen at that position is not an aromatic hydrogen
choices.why: It is an ordinary ring hydrogen. Substitution there is blocked by crowding between the two groups.

explanation: Rule 3: further substitution rarely occurs between the two groups in a meta-disubstituted compound, because this site is too hindered. So aromatic rings with three adjacent substituents must be made by some other route, such as by substitution of an ortho-disubstituted compound.

prompt: When m-chlorotoluene (methyl group on carbon 1, chlorine on carbon 3) is chlorinated with Cl2 and FeCl3, which position is rarely substituted, even though both groups direct there?

choices.text: Carbon 2, between the two groups
Carbon 4, ortho to the chlorine and para to the methyl
choices.why: Substitution at carbon 4 does occur, giving 3,4-dichlorotoluene.

choices.text: Carbon 6, ortho to the methyl and para to the chlorine
choices.why: Substitution at carbon 6 does occur, giving 2,5-dichlorotoluene.

choices.text: None; every position ortho or para to a group is substituted equally
choices.why: The position between the two groups is too hindered, so substitution there is rare.

explanation: Both groups are ortho- and para-directing, and carbon 2 is ortho to both, but it is too hindered (rule 3). Chlorination of m-chlorotoluene gives 3,4-dichlorotoluene and 2,5-dichlorotoluene instead.

prompt: Since substitution rarely occurs between the two groups of a meta-disubstituted ring, how can a ring with three adjacent substituents be prepared?

choices.text: By substitution of an ortho-disubstituted compound
By substitution of a para-disubstituted compound
choices.why: A para-disubstituted ring can't give three adjacent groups in one substitution; an ortho-disubstituted ring can.

choices.text: By heating the meta-disubstituted compound to force reaction between the groups
choices.why: The section's answer is to use a different starting compound, an ortho-disubstituted one.

choices.text: Rings with three adjacent substituents can't be made
choices.why: They can: the section says they must be prepared by some other route, such as substituting an ortho-disubstituted compound.

explanation: Aromatic rings with three adjacent substituents must be prepared by some other route than substitution between meta groups, such as by substitution of an ortho-disubstituted compound. Chlorination of o-nitrotoluene, for example, gives 2-chloro-6-nitrotoluene (along with 4-chloro-2-nitrotoluene).

prompt: Chlorination of o-nitrotoluene (Cl2, FeCl3) gives two products. Which one has three adjacent substituents?

choices.text: 2-Chloro-6-nitrotoluene
4-Chloro-2-nitrotoluene
choices.why: This is the other product, but its chlorine is para to the methyl group, not next to the other substituents.

choices.text: 3-Chloro-2-nitrotoluene
choices.why: This isn't formed: it puts chlorine ortho to the nitro group and meta to the methyl group, where neither group directs.

choices.text: 5-Chloro-2-nitrotoluene
choices.why: This isn't formed: chlorine para to the nitro group and meta to the methyl group is a position neither group directs to.

explanation: In o-nitrotoluene, the methyl group directs ortho and para to itself, and the nitro group directs meta to itself. Both effects point to the same two positions, giving 2-chloro-6-nitrotoluene (methyl flanked by nitro and chlorine) and 4-chloro-2-nitrotoluene.

prompt: What product would you expect from the bromination of p-methylbenzoic acid with Br2 and FeBr3?

choices.text: 3-Bromo-4-methylbenzoic acid
2-Bromo-4-methylbenzoic acid
choices.why: That puts bromine ortho to –CO2H and meta to –CH3, a position neither group directs to.

choices.text: 4-(Bromomethyl)benzoic acid
choices.why: Br2 and FeBr3 substitute a ring hydrogen, not a hydrogen on the methyl group.

choices.text: A mixture of 2-bromo- and 3-bromo-4-methylbenzoic acid
choices.why: Both groups direct to the position next to the methyl group, so one product forms.

explanation: Worked Example 16.5.1: the carboxyl group (–CO2H) is a meta director, and the methyl group is an ortho and para director. Both direct bromination to the position next to the methyl group, giving 3-bromo-4-methylbenzoic acid.

prompt: Where would you expect electrophilic substitution to occur on m-bromoanisole (1-bromo-3-methoxybenzene)?

choices.text: Ortho and para to the –OCH3 group
Only at carbon 5, meta to both groups
choices.why: Both groups are ortho and para directors, so neither sends the electrophile to the position meta to both.

choices.text: At the carbon bearing the bromine, replacing it
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen, not a halogen.

choices.text: Nowhere, because the bromine deactivates the ring too strongly
choices.why: Bromine is only weakly deactivating, and –OCH3 is a strong activator.

explanation: Exercise 16.5.1a: an alkoxyl group is an activator whose strong resonance donation outweighs its inductive withdrawal, while bromine is a deactivator. The more powerful activating group dominates (rule 2), so substitution occurs ortho and para to –OCH3.

prompt: Where would you expect electrophilic substitution to occur on o-bromoaniline (2-bromoaniline)?

choices.text: Ortho and para to the –NH2 group
Ortho and para to the –Br group
choices.why: Bromine is deactivating, while the amino group is a strong activator, so –NH2 controls the orientation.

choices.text: At the carbon bearing the bromine, replacing it
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen, not a halogen.

choices.text: Nowhere, because the bromine deactivates the ring too strongly
choices.why: Halogens are only weakly deactivating, and the –NH2 group strongly activates the ring.

explanation: Exercise 16.5.1b: –NH2 is a strong ortho- and para-directing activator, and –Br is a weakly deactivating ortho and para director. The more powerful activating group dominates, so substitution occurs ortho and para to –NH2.

prompt: Where would you expect electrophilic substitution to occur on o-chloronitrobenzene (1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene)?

choices.text: Ortho and para to the –Cl group
Ortho and para to the –NO2 group
choices.why: –NO2 is a meta director, so it doesn't send the electrophile ortho or para to itself.

choices.text: Nowhere, because a ring with two deactivating groups can't react
choices.why: Halogens are only weakly deactivating, and the book's answer places substitution ortho and para to –Cl.

choices.text: At the two positions adjacent to the nitro group only
choices.why: One of those positions is the chlorine-bearing carbon; the other is ortho to the nitro group, where –NO2 doesn't direct.

explanation: Exercise 16.5.1c: chlorine directs ortho and para to itself, and the nitro group directs meta to itself. The positions ortho and para to –Cl are also meta to –NO2, so the two effects reinforce each other.

prompt: o-Methylanisole (1-methoxy-2-methylbenzene) is nitrated with HNO3 and H2SO4. Where does reaction occur?

choices.text: Ortho and para to the –OCH3 group
Ortho and para to the –CH3 group
choices.why: Both groups are activators, but the alkoxyl group, with its strong resonance donation, is the more powerful one and dominates.

choices.text: Nowhere, because the two opposing activators cancel each other
choices.why: Opposing groups don't cancel. Substitution occurs, mainly where the more powerful activator directs.

choices.text: Equally at all four open ring positions
choices.why: The groups' directing effects oppose each other, and the more powerful activator, –OCH3, has the dominant influence.

explanation: Exercise 16.5.2: with o-methylanisole, reaction with either CH3CH2Cl/AlCl3 or HNO3/H2SO4 occurs ortho and para to the –OCH3 group. When directing effects oppose, the more powerful activating group dominates (rule 2), just as –OH beats –CH3 in p-methylphenol.

prompt: p-Nitroanisole has a –OCH3 group and a –NO2 group para to each other. Where does electrophilic substitution occur?

choices.text: Ortho to the –OCH3 group, which is also meta to the –NO2 group
Ortho to the –NO2 group, which is also meta to the –OCH3 group
choices.why: –NO2 is a meta director and –OCH3 an ortho/para director; neither directs to the positions next to the nitro group.

choices.text: At the carbon bearing the nitro group, replacing it
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen, not a nitro group.

choices.text: At all four open positions equally
choices.why: The two groups reinforce each other, so substitution goes to the positions ortho to –OCH3.

explanation: –OCH3 directs ortho and para (its para position is taken), and –NO2 directs meta to itself. The positions ortho to –OCH3 are exactly the positions meta to –NO2, so the effects reinforce each other (rule 1), as in p-nitrotoluene. Those two positions are equivalent, so a single product forms.
